title: Photography direction for a small consultancy
metaTitle: Photography for a small consultancy site
excerpt: Photograph the problem you take, such as the decision and its artifact. A collage of industries is range, not proof. The picture has to argue without the headline.
alt: A dim desk with an iMac showing a code editor beside a portfolio page, a second monitor with a mountain wallpaper, and a lit lamp, a busy desk that is not yet the problem.
caption: A busy desk shows work in general. The picture should show the decision. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should photographs on a consultancy site show?
faqs.answer: Show the problem you take: the artifact, the decision, or the person who runs the session with that artifact. A buyer comparing you with doing the work themselves does not need a collage of industries. They need evidence that a choice gets made.

faqs.question: Why reject a grid of sectors?
faqs.answer: It restates range, which is why the buyer thinks they can keep the work in-house. They already know their sector. Put a setting inside a single proof only when it changes the constraint. Do not lead the site with every setting you have visited.

faqs.question: How should alt text be written?
faqs.answer: Describe the frame, then the claim, as if the image did not load. Do not write a slogan. A screen-reader user should hear the scene. If words sit on the photo, keep the problem sentence readable or move the type off the image.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Small consultancy website photography should show the problem you actually take. A collage of industries does not. The pictures are part of the argument, not a mood pasted under the headline. Nielsen Norman Group's research says the first 10 seconds decide whether people stay, and many leave within 10 to 20 seconds. In those seconds the largest picture is read with the sentence. If the picture is a grid of clinics, factories, and laptops, the sentence about one decision never gets a fair hearing. A buyer comparing you with doing the work themselves already has a camera roll of their own sector. They do not need yours.

Choose frames that would still make the problem true if the words were removed. A marked-up price list. A session table with one page and too many empty chairs removed. The notes they can send the next morning. If a frame could illustrate any firm, it is costume.

## The picture is a claim about the problem

Every photograph claims something. A tasteful lounge claims you have taste. A row of sector photos claims range. A desk with a real artifact claims a decision. The buyer who might do this themselves is not shopping for taste or range. They are shopping for the end of a delay. The picture has to take their side of that comparison.

Write the claim before you choose a frame. "We force a pricing decision a founder has been rewriting." Then ask which picture survives without the sentence. The crossed-out columns. The single list. Not a skyline, not a handshake, not a mosaic labeled healthcare, logistics, and software. If you cannot name the frame, you are not ready to art-direct. You are ready to buy a mood.

One claim per page. The homepage picture supports the problem. A proof picture supports the decision and its cost. An about picture supports the person who will be in the session, at the work, not on a mountain. Do not reuse a lounge because the interior was expensive. Expense is not the problem.

W3C's WCAG 2 overview treats images as content, under principles that begin with perceivable. A picture that carries the argument has to be described, and it has to sit still long enough to be read with the sentence. A carousel of sectors spends the first 10 seconds on motion and range. One still image, chosen, is the stronger claim.

## Reject the industry collage

The collage is the industry list as photography. Six squares, six sectors, a caption about breadth. It reassures the partners that no buyer is excluded. The buyer reads it as generic, which is the reason they keep the work in-house. They know their sector better than a grid does. Delete the collage even if a designer spent a day on the crop.

Reject the same substitutes. A handshake. A city avenue. A sculpture in a lobby. A celebration. A wall of smiling professionals who are not the decision. These are collages with one tile. They claim "business" without a problem. A buyer who has postponed a decision has seen all of them on firms that sold hours and left the choice undone.

Reject a portrait that is only a lifestyle. The person may be in the frame if the artifact is in the frame. Their hobby, their city, their coffee, are not the problem. A dim desk with a screen full of unrelated work is the same mistake: it shows that someone is busy, not that a decision was forced. Busy is what the buyer already is.

If a board member wants the sectors visible, put a true setting inside a proof where it changes the constraint, one story at a time. Do not put all the settings in the header. Range can be true and still be the wrong picture for the first screen.

## A shot list from the problem

Build the list from the stuck thing, not from a portfolio of interiors.

- The artifact before and after the decision, if you can show it without exposing a client. Crossed-out options. One remaining page. The sentence they will use.
- The session as work: a table, the page, the pen, the empty chair of the person who almost did not attend. Not a staged laugh.
- The person who runs the session, with the artifact, named in the caption if the about page names them. Hands in frame are useful. A seamless backdrop is not.
- The buyer's kind of mess, photographed as evidence, not as poverty. A spreadsheet is allowed if it is the real stuck object. Glamour is not required. Legibility is.

Six frames can carry a small site. You do not need a library. You need the homepage, one proof, and the person. Extra frames become a sector carousel the week someone feels the site looks thin. Thin and true is better than full and generic.

If you take two problems, shoot both, and do not blend them in one hero. Pricing notes and a hiring scorecard in one frame look like the collage again. Separate pages, separate pictures.

## What to tell the photographer

Send the problem sentence, the list of rejects, and two references that are about subject. Say what must be readable. Say which client artifacts are forbidden. Ask for stills. A film that opens on a city usually returns the collage as motion. A still you can judge is enough.

Stay for the first setups. The wrong frame is obvious early: the photographer reaches for a meeting, a window, a smile. Stop it. Do not accept it later out of politeness. Name files by the problem, not by a camera number, so the collage does not get reattached by the next person who touches the site.

Pay for the usage you need, and keep files you can crop. A picture you cannot recrop will bully the phone layout. The meaningful part has to survive a narrow width. If the decision is in the corner of a wide room, it will be cropped away. Move the subject to the center or do not use the frame as a hero.

## Alt text and captions

Write alt text from the frame, then the claim. "A one-page price list with two columns crossed out, on a homepage about a pricing decision." If the image fails, the sentence still works. "Consulting excellence" does not, and it stuffs a mood into a description a screen reader will say aloud.

Captions can name the decision. "The fifth price, refused in the room." That caption works. "Our approach" does not. Credit stock or a photographer when it is not your picture. Do not imply a stock factory is a client.

If type sits on the photograph, check that the problem sentence remains readable. WCAG's perceivable principle fails when the words disappear into a bright window. Move the type to a plain ground rather than dimming the picture into mud. A muddy hero is still the largest thing on the screen, and now it is illegible.

## A review with the headline covered

Cover the words and show the homepage picture to someone who has the problem. Ask what the firm takes. If they say "a nice office" or "lots of industries," the frame failed. If they say the decision, or even "someone is choosing," the frame is close enough to design around. Do this before you pay for a second shoot. It is cheaper than discovering the collage in the live site.

Do the same with the proof image. The person should be able to point at the cost. A smile is not a cost. A crossed-out option is. If they cannot find it, the picture is atmosphere and the paragraph is doing all the work. Either reshoot or drop the picture and let the paragraph be the proof. A page with one honest image is calmer than a page that decorates every section. Calm is appropriate. This buyer is already overstimulated by their own unfinished decision. Do not add noise.

## When stock is honest, and when it is a costume

Stock is honest when it shows the artifact or a typical version of the mess, and you do not pretend it is a named client. A generic spreadsheet is a weak picture but an honest one if your problem is a spreadsheet and you say so. Stock is a costume when it is a sector mosaic, a handshake, or a diverse meeting that could illustrate any essay about work. Those pictures are empty on purpose. Emptiness is what this buyer is trained to notice.

If you cannot shoot this month, publish fewer pictures. One true artifact and open space beats a grid of industries. Add frames when a session produces something you are allowed to show. Do not fill the grid to make the design look finished. The grid is how the industry list returns after you removed it from the navigation.

The frames also have to survive a phone, where the crop will cut the corner you thought was a detail. Read [how the first screen has to hold the problem on a phone](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-a-small-consultancy) before you approve a wide photograph that only works on a desktop.

If you want a second opinion on whether a frame claims a problem or a mood, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the picture without the headline. If the problem is not visible, the picture is not ready.
